tagline.text: The first contemporary art museum in the Visayas and Mindanao, an arts anchor in Iloilo Business Park

location.label: Location
location.text: Casa de Emperador, Iloilo Business Park, Mandurriao, Iloilo City

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (a good indoor plan on rainy days)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–600 (admission plus a simple meal and transport)

children.text: The Iloilo Museum of Contemporary Art (ILOMOCA) opened in March 2018 as the first museum in the Visayas and Mindanao devoted to contemporary art. Its three floors and five exhibit halls show works by Ilonggo artists, pieces by Dalí, Chagall and Miró, and glass sculpture.

The Iloilo Museum of Contemporary Art, ILOMOCA for short, stands inside Iloilo Business Park in Mandurriao, on the western side of Iloilo City. It opened on March 17, 2018, and is described as the first museum in the Visayas and Mindanao dedicated solely to modern art. Megaworld, the developer of this 72-hectare township, built it through the Megaworld Foundation in partnership with art collector Edwin Valencia. Valencia began collecting in the 1980s while working as an investment banker in New York, and is said to have suggested Iloilo rather than Manila as the home for the collection.
The building is called Casa de Emperador, and right next door is the Brandy Museum, the country's first, run by Emperador Brandy. The construction cost is reported at about
(some sources say ₱110,000,000), and the building covers roughly
3,000 square meters
across three floors and five exhibit halls, linked by escalators. In front stands a

bronze equestrian statue of General Martin Delgado, Iloilo's first Filipino governor, which makes a handy meeting point. It is the work of Spanish sculptor Ginés Serrán-Pagán: the general rides with a sword in his left hand, and a dove rising above his shoulder symbolizes the fight for freedom.

For travelers, the museum's appeal is simple: it is a place to see real contemporary art in the Visayas. The ground-floor Hulot hall hosts rotating shows by local and international artists. On the second floor, The Gallery presents works by Ilonggo artists, masters such as Salvador Dalí, Marc Chagall and Joan Miró, and Ramon Orlina's glass sculptures, each in its own themed room. The third-floor Adoracion Valencia Gallery displays works from the Valencia family collection, including pieces by National Artists Arturo Luz and Ang Kiukok. At its opening, about 125 works loaned by Valencia were reported to be on show.

This guide is for travelers who want a few hours of indoor art between sightseeing in Iloilo City or a trip to Miagao Church. The visit itself takes one to two hours, and you can extend it into a full day with the malls and restaurants in the same business park. Exhibitions change on a set schedule, so check the official social media pages or website for what is on before you go. Admission and hours here were matched against the official website and a travel guide, but hours and prices can change, so it is safest to confirm the latest announcement before you visit.
This bronze equestrian statue, about

tall, stands in front of the building and honors Martin Delgado, Iloilo's first Filipino governor. It is the work of Spanish artist Ginés Serrán-Pagán and is the museum's signature photo spot. Walk around it once before you go in and look at the horse's musculature and the sculpted dove.

This exhibition space presents work by local and international artists. It connects to a sales area where artists can sell directly, work honoring General Delgado, and the museum shop. Part of the lobby is open free of charge, so if you are short on time you can take a quick look here alone.

This is the most regional room on the second floor, bringing together artists from Western Visayas such as Rock Drilon, Ed Defensor, Nelfa Querubin and Ofelia Gelvezon-Tequi. Paintings that retell Iloilo's landscapes, people and faith through a contemporary lens help you understand the city's character.

This room shows works by international masters such as Salvador Dalí, Marc Chagall, Joan Miró and Victor Vasarely. Contemporary artists such as Bruno Catalano have also been shown alongside them. It is a rare chance to see European modern art up close on a Philippine island.

This room collects work by Ramon Orlina, known for his glass sculpture, and by sculptors such as Alab Pagarigan, Benedicto Cabrera (BenCab) and Ferdinand Cacnio. Glass pieces that shift color in the light make good photographs. Natural-light photography is allowed only in the lobby and on the porch balcony, so please follow the rules.

This permanent-collection room on the third floor is named after the mother of founding patron Edwin Valencia. From the Valencia family holdings you can see major works of Philippine contemporary art, including pieces by National Artists Arturo Luz and Ang Kiukok.

This small performance and screening space on the second floor is used for theater, performance art, workshops and cultural events. It holds roughly 50 to 60 people. If the timing works, you may catch a small performance or screening alongside the exhibits, so check the event listings on the official social media pages.
The museum shop sells items inspired by the artworks, and a curator or docent can guide you if you arrange it in advance by phone. For group visits, it helps to call ahead and set a schedule.

items.title: Half-day plan
items.subtitle: Museum visit and a stroll through the business park

children.text: Arrive at opening time, look over the Delgado statue and the building's exterior, then buy your ticket at the counter. Leave large bags at the baggage counter.
See the ground-floor Hulot hall and the museum shop, then take the escalator to the second floor. Show your ticket stub to the security guard at the second-floor entrance.
Visit The Gallery's Ilonggo Country room, the international masters room and the sculpture gallery in turn.
Enjoy the permanent collection at the third-floor Adoracion Valencia Gallery.
Have lunch at the dining area in the business park, then look around the neighboring Brandy Museum or the mall.
Viewing time varies with the exhibitions, but
1–2 hours
is usually enough. The museum is closed on Mondays, so check before you plan your day.

items.title: One-day plan combined with Iloilo City
items.subtitle: From heritage to contemporary art

children.text: Set out from your hotel and see the old streets and churches of the city. Visit one or two sights first, such as Jaro Cathedral or Molo Church.
Eat lunch in the city or at the business park and rest for the afternoon.
Take a taxi or Grab to Iloilo Business Park and visit ILOMOCA.
Have coffee at the neighboring Brandy Museum or the mall, and after sunset stroll along the Iloilo River Esplanade.
This plan pairs Spanish-era heritage with contemporary art in one day, so the contrast is clear. Travel time depends on traffic.
There are several direct flights a day from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), and the flight takes about
1 hour 10 to 25 minutes
(per two flight-information sites; Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific and AirAsia fly the route). Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
Iloilo International Airport is in Cabatuan, away from the city, so you reach the city or the business park by taxi, Grab or an airport shuttle. Check travel time and fares locally.
You can also travel from Manila by ferry or bus, but the trip is long, so most people fly.
From Iloilo City proper, a taxi or Grab is the easiest option. Enter Casa de Emperador on Festive Walk Parade in Iloilo Business Park as your destination.
Jeepneys and other city transport also run, but the routes are confusing, so first-timers are better off with a taxi or Grab. Check fares locally.

The museum is in the same development as Festive Walk Mall, so you can walk to it from hotels, malls and restaurants inside the park. When it rains, ask about covered mall passages you can use to get there.

ILOMOCA is an indoor attraction, so you can visit all year. Iloilo has many clear days in the dry season from December to May, which suits combining the museum with a city walking tour, while in the rainy season from June to November it makes a good indoor plan to avoid showers.

Exhibitions change on a schedule, so if there is a particular artist or show you want to see, set your date around it. The whole city gets crowded during Dinagyang, Iloilo's signature festival held in late January, so book lodging and transport early.

Iloilo Business Park, where ILOMOCA stands, is a mixed-use development of hotels, shopping malls and offices. Hotels such as the Marriott and Richmonde make it convenient if you plan to stay around your museum visit, and getting to Iloilo International Airport and the city is easy by taxi or Grab. Hotel names and rates change a lot by season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

Food is easy to find at the restaurants, food courts and cafes in the park's malls. Iloilo is famous for La Paz batchoy, pancit molo (Molo soup) and chicken inasal, so try each when you head into the city. Eating and drinking are not allowed inside the museum, so have your meals before or after your visit.
The museum is closed on Mondays and open Tuesday to Sunday from
to
. The museum shop is said to stay open until
Large bags and backpacks are not allowed in, so leave them at the baggage counter or in your vehicle or hotel. Bags are searched.
Do not touch the artworks, keep your voice down and silence your phone. Smoking and bringing in food or drink are prohibited indoors.
Photography is allowed only with natural light in the lobby and on the porch balcony, and selfie sticks are not allowed. Follow on-site signs for photography in the galleries.
When you go up to the second floor, show your ticket stub to the security guard. Keep it so you do not lose it.
Arrange docent tours in advance by calling the museum. For group visits, it helps to tell staff your schedule and group size.
Check the official social media pages (@ILOMOCA) or website for current exhibitions and events. Pets are not allowed inside.
The interior is air-conditioned and can feel cool, so bring a light layer.
Opening hours, prices and exhibition schedules can change. Check the latest announcement on the official website or social media before you go.
The museum is closed on Mondays, so it is easy to make a wasted trip. Check the day of the week before you add it to your plan.
During exhibition changeovers, some galleries may close or the works on display may differ. If you want to see a particular artist, ask in advance.
Large bags, tripods and selfie sticks are restricted. Keep valuables on you and leave large luggage at your hotel.
In a taxi, check whether the meter is used, and for Grab, enter your destination in the app accurately.
The information in this guide covers what could be confirmed as of 2026, and prices are higher than at opening (₱100).
This central city of Western Visayas, with Spanish-era buildings, great food and markets, lets you walk to many historic sights within
Iloilo City
. Take a taxi from the business park.
This riverside promenade, the
Iloilo River Esplanade
, is pleasant for a walk around sunset. It connects to the modern business district, making it a fitting stroll after the museum.
One of Iloilo's best-known churches,
Jaro Cathedral
offers an old-world facade and a lively plaza atmosphere. It pairs well with the museum in a single day.
This Gothic-style stone church,
Molo Church
, shows off Iloilo's architectural heritage. Seeing old architecture in contrast with contemporary art makes the day richer.
